category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: Default initialization vs. value initialization
description: Different initialization syntaxes have different rules for fundamental types, aggregates, and classes. Assuming all declarations produce initialized values can be dangerous.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: The most vexing parse
description: C++ grammar can interpret something that appears to construct an object as a function declaration instead.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: Brace initialization vs. parentheses
description: Using braces can select different constructors than using parentheses, particularly when `std::initializer_list` is involved.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: Initializer-list constructor preference
description: Constructors accepting `std::initializer_list` receive special treatment during overload resolution and can unexpectedly take precedence over other constructors.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: Narrowing conversions
description: Brace initialization rejects certain conversions that other initialization forms permit, while ordinary implicit conversions can silently lose information.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: Implicit conversion chains
description: User-defined conversions, converting constructors, and standard conversions interact in ways that make overload selection non-obvious.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: `explicit` constructors and conversion operators
description: Explicitness affects some initialization and contextual conversion forms but not others.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: Null pointer overload resolution
description: `0`, `NULL`, and `nullptr` have different types and conversion behavior, producing surprising overload resolution results.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: Integer literal type deduction
description: The type of an integer literal depends on its value, base, and suffix, potentially changing the selected overload.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: Aggregate initialization and member ordering
description: Aggregate initialization follows structural rules that can make changes to member declarations silently change program behavior.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: Class member initialization order
description: Members are initialized in declaration order, not the textual order of a constructor's member-initializer list.

category: Initialization and implicit conversions
title: Class template argument deduction (CTAD)
description: Deduction guides and constructor-based deduction can infer types different from those a programmer expects.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: `auto` drops qualifiers and references
description: Ordinary `auto` deduction can discard top-level `const` and reference qualification, accidentally introducing copies or permitting mutation.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: `auto` with brace initialization
description: Direct-list and copy-list initialization have special deduction rules that differ from ordinary expressions.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: `decltype` vs. `decltype(auto)`
description: These follow rules different from ordinary `auto`, and subtle expression changes can turn a value return into a reference return.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: Parentheses changing `decltype` results
description: `decltype` distinguishes certain unparenthesized expressions from general expressions, making seemingly insignificant parentheses affect the deduced type.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: Lvalues, prvalues, and xvalues
description: Expression value categories determine binding, overload selection, lifetime behavior, and move eligibility.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: Reference collapsing
description: Combinations of lvalue and rvalue references follow specific collapsing rules that are essential to template deduction.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: Forwarding references vs. rvalue references
description: Similar-looking reference declarations can have very different deduction and binding behavior.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: Incorrect `std::forward` usage
description: Forwarding a value with the wrong template argument can change its value category and lead to unintended moves.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: Const rvalues and move semantics
description: A `const` object may not be movable through an ordinary move constructor even when explicitly cast to an rvalue.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: Reference-qualified member functions
description: Member functions qualified with `&`, `&&`, or `const` participate in overload resolution based on the value category and qualifiers of the object.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: `std::move` is only a cast
description: Applying `std::move` doesn't itself move an object, and the eventual operation may still copy.

category: Type deduction, references, and value categories
title: Perfect-forwarding constructors hijacking overloads
description: An unconstrained forwarding-reference constructor can unexpectedly compete with or override intended copy and converting constructors.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Returning references or pointers to local objects
description: References and pointers do not extend the lifetime of objects whose storage has ended.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Temporary lifetime extension
description: Binding a temporary to a reference extends its lifetime in certain situations, but several syntactically similar situations are exceptions.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Reference members bound to temporaries
description: Initializing references stored inside objects has lifetime rules that differ depending on the initialization context.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: `std::string_view` dangling references
description: A `string_view` does not own characters, and implicit conversions from strings can disguise lifetime problems.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: `std::span` ownership confusion
description: A `span` carries a pointer and extent, not ownership, and can outlive or become invalidated by its backing storage.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: `std::initializer_list` backing-array lifetime
description: An initializer list references a temporary array whose lifetime is not always as long as the list object.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Dangling lambda captures
description: Capturing a local variable by reference creates lifetime hazards when the closure escapes its defining scope.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Capturing `this` in lambdas
description: Capturing `this` does not generally preserve the containing object's lifetime, and copy-capture defaults can be misleading.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Dangling `c_str()` and `data()` pointers
description: Pointers obtained from strings can become invalid when the string is modified or destroyed.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Lifetime of subobjects and base objects
description: A subobject's validity depends on the lifetime and construction/destruction state of its enclosing object.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Range-based `for` over temporary objects
description: Lifetime extension in range-based loops has subtle rules, including important differences between C++20 and C++23.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Proxy references
description: Some iterators and accessors return proxy objects rather than actual references, making binding and lifetime assumptions unreliable.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Destructor and temporary destruction timing
description: Temporaries normally die at full-expression boundaries, while local variables and members have specific reverse-destruction orders.

category: Object lifetime, temporaries, and dangling references
title: Returning a reference through multiple function calls
description: A chain of apparently safe reference-returning functions can conceal an object that dies along the way.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Reading uninitialized values
description: Objects with indeterminate or erroneous values can trigger undefined or erroneous behavior, depending on type and language version.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Strict aliasing violations
description: Accessing an object through an unrelated type can violate type-access rules, even when the memory representation is compatible.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: `reinterpret_cast` doesn't create objects
description: Reinterpreting a pointer's type does not automatically create an object of that type or begin its lifetime.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Misaligned accesses
description: A pointer can refer to sufficient memory yet still be invalid for accessing a type whose alignment requirements aren't met.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Pointer arithmetic outside an array
description: Pointer arithmetic is only defined within tightly specified object and array bounds, not arbitrary nearby allocated memory.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: One-past-the-end pointers
description: Constructing certain one-past pointers is legal, but dereferencing them is not.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Pointer provenance and lifetime
description: Numerical equality of addresses is insufficient to prove that a pointer is valid for accessing an object.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Union type punning
description: Reading an inactive union member can violate C++ lifetime and type-access rules, even when a compiler accepts it as an extension.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Placement new and object replacement
description: Reusing storage requires understanding when the old object's lifetime ends and the new object's lifetime begins.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: `std::launder` and pointer reuse
description: After certain object replacements, an existing pointer cannot simply be used to access the new object without satisfying special rules.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: `memcpy` on non-trivial types
description: Byte-copying an object does not generally reproduce the semantics of copy construction or assignment.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Raw allocation vs. object construction
description: Allocating enough bytes for a type is not always equivalent to constructing an object of that type.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Struct padding and object representations
description: Structures may contain padding bytes, so binary comparisons or serialization of complete object representations may be misleading.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Object layout and `offsetof` assumptions
description: Standard-layout guarantees are narrower than many programmers expect, particularly with inheritance and polymorphism.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Mismatched allocation and deallocation
description: Mixing allocation/deallocation mechanisms or array and scalar deletion operations can cause undefined behavior.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Invalid pointer use after deallocation
description: Freed storage does not remain a valid object merely because its address is still held in a pointer.

category: Raw memory, pointers, aliasing, and the C++ object model
title: Over-aligned allocation and packed structures
description: Nonstandard alignment assumptions or packed representations can produce invalid accesses when pointers to members escape.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Signed integer overflow
description: Overflow of ordinary signed integer arithmetic is generally undefined behavior, enabling optimizations that surprise programmers.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Unsigned arithmetic wraparound
description: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo its range, which is defined but can still create subtle indexing and arithmetic bugs.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Signed/unsigned comparisons
description: Usual arithmetic conversions can produce surprising outcomes when signed and unsigned values interact.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Integer promotions
description: Smaller integral types are promoted before many arithmetic operations, changing intermediate types and results.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Integer division corner cases
description: Division by zero and certain signed division overflows have undefined behavior.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Bit shifts and signed integers
description: Shift counts, operand promotions, and signed-shift semantics have rules that differ across language versions.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Truncation and overflow during numeric casts
description: Integral and floating-point conversions can truncate, change signedness, or enter undefined-behavior territory.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Character signedness
description: Whether plain `char` is signed is implementation-defined, which can break arithmetic and byte-oriented logic.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Unsequenced side effects
description: Multiple modifications or reads of the same scalar object within an expression can become undefined behavior when sequencing requirements are violated.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Function argument evaluation order
description: Function arguments are not generally evaluated in a guaranteed left-to-right order, even though C++17 strengthened certain sequencing rules.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Operator precedence vs. evaluation order
description: Parsing precedence, associativity, and runtime evaluation sequencing are different concepts.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Conditional operator type deduction
description: The conditional operator applies complex rules to determine common types and value categories, sometimes creating unexpected conversions or temporaries.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: Floating-point non-associativity
description: Reordering floating-point arithmetic can alter numerical results, and compiler optimization settings can change the effective guarantees.

category: Arithmetic, bitwise operations, and expression evaluation
title: NaN and comparison semantics
description: NaN breaks ordinary ordering intuitions and can violate comparator requirements used by standard algorithms and containers.

category: Classes, inheritance, virtual functions, and destruction
title: Object slicing
description: Copying a derived object into a base object by value discards the derived portion and changes polymorphic behavior.

category: Classes, inheritance, virtual functions, and destruction
title: Deleting through a non-virtual base destructor
description: Destroying a derived object through an incompatible base-class deletion interface can cause undefined behavior.

category: Classes, inheritance, virtual functions, and destruction
title: Virtual calls during construction and destruction
description: Virtual dispatch is restricted by the object's current construction or destruction stage rather than always reaching the most-derived override.

category: Classes, inheritance, virtual functions, and destruction
title: Pure virtual calls in object lifetime transitions
description: Calling a pure virtual function in an inappropriate construction/destruction context can result in undefined behavior.

category: Classes, inheritance, virtual functions, and destruction
title: Default arguments on virtual functions
description: Virtual dispatch and default argument selection use different binding mechanisms, producing counterintuitive results.

category: Classes, inheritance, virtual functions, and destruction
title: Name hiding in inheritance
description: A declaration in a derived class can hide base-class overloads even when the parameter lists differ.

category: Classes, inheritance, virtual functions, and destruction
title: Multiple inheritance pointer adjustments
description: Converting between base and derived pointers can require address adjustment rather than a simple reinterpretation.

category: Classes, inheritance, virtual functions, and destruction
title: Virtual inheritance layout assumptions
description: Virtual bases complicate object layout, pointer offsets, and the assumptions behind low-level casts.

category: Classes, inheritance, virtual functions, and destruction
title: RTTI during construction or destruction
description: `dynamic_cast` and `typeid` interact with the object's current construction/destruction state, not just its eventual dynamic type.

category: Classes, inheritance, virtual functions, and destruction
title: Shallow `const` and logical constness
description: `const` on a pointer-like wrapper or object does not necessarily imply that all reachable data is immutable.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: Use-after-move assumptions
description: A moved-from object is generally still valid but has an unspecified state unless its type provides stronger guarantees.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: Moving from `const` objects
description: Ordinary move operations often cannot bind to `const` sources, silently causing copies.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: Pessimizing moves on return
description: Explicitly applying `std::move` to a local return object can inhibit named return value optimization.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: Copy elision vs. actual moves
description: Guaranteed copy elision and optional NRVO differ, and reasoning in terms of an invisible move constructor can be incorrect.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: Implicitly deleted or suppressed special members
description: Declaring one special member function can affect generation or availability of copy and move constructors and assignments.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: Exception safety of move constructors
description: Whether moves can throw influences how standard containers relocate objects and preserve exception guarantees.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: Double ownership with `std::shared_ptr`
description: Constructing independent owning control blocks for the same raw object can cause multiple deletions.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: `shared_ptr` ownership cycles
description: Reference-counted ownership cannot reclaim strongly connected cycles without deliberately breaking the ownership graph.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: `enable_shared_from_this` misuse
description: Requesting shared ownership from an object not properly managed by a compatible shared control block can fail.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: `weak_ptr` check-then-use races
description: Checking whether an object is expired does not reserve its lifetime; obtaining temporary ownership requires the appropriate operation.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: `unique_ptr::release` vs. `reset`
description: These operations have fundamentally different ownership and destruction effects.

category: Move semantics, ownership, and RAII
title: Self-move and aliasing in assignment
description: Move assignment must respect the type's requirements even when source and destination refer to the same object.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: `std::vector` reallocation invalidation
description: Growth may invalidate every pointer, reference, and iterator into a vector.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: `reserve()` vs. `resize()`
description: Capacity and constructed element count are distinct, and confusing them can lead to accesses outside the valid element range.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: `std::deque` invalidation rules
description: Deque iterator and reference invalidation rules differ significantly from vector and list rules and depend on the operation.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: `std::unordered_map` rehashing
description: Rehashing invalidates iterators while preserving certain references and pointers, a distinction that is easy to miss.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: Past-the-end iterator invalidation
description: A cached `end()` iterator may become invalid after container modification even when some element iterators remain valid.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: Erasing while iterating
description: Container-specific invalidation rules can make ordinary increment-and-erase loops invalid.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: `std::map::operator[]` implicit insertion
description: Access using `operator[]` can mutate the container even when the programmer intended a read-only lookup.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: `insert`, `emplace`, and `try_emplace` semantics
description: These operations differ in construction, evaluation, and handling of existing keys.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: Strict weak ordering requirements
description: Invalid comparison predicates can violate associative-container or sorting-algorithm preconditions, potentially causing undefined behavior.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: Hash/equality consistency
description: Unordered containers require hashing and equality to agree on equivalent keys.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: `std::vector<bool>` specialization
description: Its bit-packed storage and proxy-reference behavior differ materially from ordinary `std::vector<T>`.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: `std::remove` vs. container erasure
description: The standard removal algorithm rearranges elements but does not itself reduce a container's size.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: Algorithms with invalid ranges or iterators
description: Standard algorithms depend on valid ranges, output destinations, and often additional ordering or overlap preconditions.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: Returning references from `std::min` and `std::max`
description: Their reference-returning overloads can create dangling results when temporaries are involved.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: `std::accumulate` initial-value type
description: The accumulator's type is determined by the initial value, which can silently affect arithmetic precision and overflow.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: `std::reduce` ordering assumptions
description: Reduction is not necessarily performed in left-to-right order, which matters for non-associative operations.

category: Standard containers, iterators, and algorithms
title: Iterator category vs. algorithmic complexity
description: Generic algorithms may compile with non-random-access iterators yet have unexpectedly poor complexity compared with container-specific operations.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: Two-phase name lookup
description: Names in templates can be resolved at different times, producing surprising differences between dependent and non-dependent expressions.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: Argument-dependent lookup (ADL)
description: Unqualified function calls can discover overloads through associated types and namespaces, changing overload selection.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: Hidden friend functions
description: Friend functions defined inside classes can participate in ADL while remaining invisible to ordinary lookup.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: Dependent `typename` and `template` disambiguation
description: The compiler sometimes needs explicit guidance to distinguish types and template names from other dependent constructs.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: SFINAE vs. hard compilation errors
description: Not every substitution failure occurs in a context where it is silently removed from overload consideration.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: Template overloads vs. specializations
description: Function-template specializations do not participate in overload selection in the same way as ordinary overloads.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: Forwarding references and braced initializer lists
description: Braced lists do not behave like ordinary deducible expressions, breaking otherwise generic forwarding interfaces.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: Implicit conversion ranking
description: Exact matches, promotions, conversions, and user-defined conversions interact with template deduction and overload ranking.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: Concepts and constraint subsumption
description: C++20 constraints don't always order overloads according to intuitive logical implications.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: `if constexpr` discarded branches
description: A discarded branch is not a blanket exemption from syntax, semantic, and template-validity requirements.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: `constexpr`, `consteval`, and `constinit`
description: These keywords impose different compile-time evaluation or initialization requirements and are not interchangeable.

category: Templates, overload resolution, and name lookup
title: Template instantiation across translation units
description: Templates that compile independently can still encounter definition visibility, specialization, or linkage problems.

category: Exceptions, error handling, and termination
title: Throwing from destructors
description: Exceptions escaping destructors during stack unwinding can cause immediate program termination.

category: Exceptions, error handling, and termination
title: `noexcept` violations
description: An exception escaping a non-throwing function results in termination rather than ordinary exception propagation.

category: Exceptions, error handling, and termination
title: Catching polymorphic exceptions by value
description: Catching by value can copy and slice an exception object, changing its observed type.

category: Exceptions, error handling, and termination
title: `throw;` vs. throwing an exception object
description: Rethrowing an active exception differs from constructing and throwing another exception, including implications for slicing.

category: Exceptions, error handling, and termination
title: Constructor exceptions and partial object destruction
description: When construction throws, destruction applies to completed subobjects, not to a fully constructed containing object.

category: Exceptions, error handling, and termination
title: `std::optional::value()` and `std::expected::value()`
description: These accessors have explicit failure behavior that differs from unchecked access and from exception-free assumptions.

category: Exceptions, error handling, and termination
title: `std::variant` exceptional states
description: Some operations can leave a variant without an active alternative, invalidating assumptions that it always holds exactly one.

category: Exceptions, error handling, and termination
title: Exception guarantees and partially modified state
description: Operations can provide basic, strong, or no meaningful exception guarantee; assuming rollback is automatic can corrupt program invariants.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Data races and undefined behavior
description: Unsynchronized conflicting accesses to the same memory location can cause undefined behavior, not merely stale or inconsistent reads.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Atomicity vs. visibility vs. ordering
description: Making an individual operation atomic does not automatically establish the synchronization needed for surrounding memory accesses.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: `memory_order_relaxed` misuse
description: Relaxed atomics preserve atomicity but do not automatically publish or synchronize other data.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Release/acquire synchronization
description: Release/acquire ordering establishes synchronization only under the relevant reads-from and ordering conditions.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Sequential consistency misconceptions
description: Even sequentially consistent atomic operations do not make an entire program behave like a single globally serialized execution in every respect.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Release sequences and read-modify-write operations
description: Release sequences have precise rules that matter when multiple threads modify a publication or synchronization variable.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Incorrect compare-exchange loops
description: `compare_exchange_weak` may fail spuriously, and both compare-exchange variants update the expected-value argument upon failure.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Invalid compare-exchange memory orders
description: Success and failure memory-order constraints differ, and violating those constraints can produce invalid atomic usage.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: ABA problem in lock-free algorithms
description: A pointer or state can return to an earlier value while the underlying object history has changed, invalidating simple compare-and-swap reasoning.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Memory reclamation in lock-free structures
description: Removing a node atomically does not guarantee it is safe to reclaim while other threads might still access it.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Condition-variable spurious wakeups
description: A waiting thread can wake without the desired condition becoming true, so wakeup alone is not proof that the invariant holds.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Lost wakeups and predicate synchronization
description: Incorrect coordination between the predicate, mutex, and notification can leave threads blocked indefinitely.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Mutex deadlock from inconsistent lock ordering
description: Acquiring multiple mutexes in conflicting orders can deadlock even if each individual operation appears correct.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: `std::thread` destruction semantics
description: Destroying a joinable `std::thread` causes program termination rather than automatically joining or detaching it.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: `std::async` execution policy surprises
description: An async task may be deferred, and associated future lifecycle operations can unexpectedly block.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Misunderstanding `volatile`
description: C++ `volatile` does not provide inter-thread synchronization or replace atomics.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Concurrent access to standard containers
description: Thread-safe independent reads do not imply that concurrent structural modifications or iterator use are safe.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Atomic reference-counting misconceptions
description: Atomic `shared_ptr` ownership management does not automatically make accesses to the managed object thread-safe.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: `std::atomic_ref` lifetime and alignment
description: Retrofitting atomic operations onto an existing object comes with alignment, lifetime, and mixed-access constraints.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: Lock-free vs. wait-free guarantees
description: An atomic operation being lock-free does not imply bounded latency, starvation freedom, or wait-free progress.

category: Concurrency, atomics, and the C++ memory model
title: False sharing
description: Independent variables occupying the same cache line can cause severe contention without any C++ data race.

category: Modern C++: ranges, coroutines, and vocabulary types
title: Lazy ranges and repeated evaluation
description: Range views can defer computation, meaning dereferencing or iterating may execute transformations at a different time or frequency than expected.

category: Modern C++: ranges, coroutines, and vocabulary types
title: Dangling range adaptors
description: Composing non-owning views can preserve references to short-lived objects without making the lifetime problem obvious.

category: Modern C++: ranges, coroutines, and vocabulary types
title: Borrowed ranges vs. owning ranges
description: Range algorithms distinguish ranges whose iterators can safely outlive the range object from those whose iterators cannot.

category: Modern C++: ranges, coroutines, and vocabulary types
title: Structured bindings and copying
description: Structured bindings can introduce copies or references depending on declaration syntax and tuple-like customization.

category: Modern C++: ranges, coroutines, and vocabulary types
title: Coroutine frame lifetime
description: Coroutines manage their own state and suspension points, so local-variable and parameter lifetimes differ from ordinary functions.

category: Modern C++: ranges, coroutines, and vocabulary types
title: Dangling coroutine captures and references
description: Captures and reference parameters may outlive their referents across suspension, even when the coroutine frame remains valid.

category: Modern C++: ranges, coroutines, and vocabulary types
title: Coroutine handle ownership
description: Coroutine handles are non-owning interfaces, making destruction, resumption, and double-destruction hazards particularly important.

category: Modern C++: ranges, coroutines, and vocabulary types
title: Suspending while holding locks
description: Suspending a coroutine while retaining thread-affine synchronization resources can lead to deadlocks or invalid resumption assumptions.

category: Modern C++: ranges, coroutines, and vocabulary types
title: `std::optional` disengaged-state access
description: Optional objects distinguish between being present and holding a particular value, with different rules for checked and unchecked access.

category: Modern C++: ranges, coroutines, and vocabulary types
title: `std::any` and `std::variant` runtime type assumptions
description: These types offer different forms of type erasure and discriminated storage, and invalid access has different failure semantics.

category: Translation units, linkage, initialization, and ABI

description: Inconsistent or duplicated definitions across translation units can produce ill-formed programs, sometimes without a required diagnostic.

category: Translation units, linkage, initialization, and ABI
title: Static initialization order fiasco
description: Dynamically initialized objects in different translation units may depend on initialization ordering that is not guaranteed.

category: Translation units, linkage, initialization, and ABI
title: Static destruction order
description: Objects with static storage duration can be destroyed in an order that invalidates dependencies still used by other destructors.

category: Translation units, linkage, initialization, and ABI
title: Function-local static initialization
description: Initialization of local statics is thread-safe under modern C++ rules, but recursion during initialization has special hazards.

category: Translation units, linkage, initialization, and ABI
title: `inline` functions and variables across translation units
description: `inline` changes ODR and linkage rules rather than simply requesting that a compiler eliminate function calls.

category: Translation units, linkage, initialization, and ABI
title: Header-defined globals and linkage
description: Namespaces, `static`, `extern`, `const`, and inline variables have different linkage behaviors that can create duplicate or independent objects.

category: Translation units, linkage, initialization, and ABI
title: ABI incompatibility
description: Object layout, calling conventions, name mangling, exception handling, and standard-library ABI choices can prevent separately compiled binaries from interoperating safely.

category: Translation units, linkage, initialization, and ABI
title: Mismatched compiler flags across translation units
description: Differences in macro definitions, structure packing, ABI modes, or language configuration can silently invalidate cross-file assumptions.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: Hidden dynamic allocations
description: High-level library abstractions can allocate internally despite looking inexpensive at the call site.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: `std::function` type-erasure overhead
description: Type erasure can introduce indirect calls, potentially hidden allocations, and implementation-dependent small-object storage behavior.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: Virtual dispatch and devirtualization
description: Virtual calls can obstruct some optimizations, but the actual cost depends on whether the compiler can devirtualize and inline them.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: `std::shared_ptr` reference-count contention
description: Shared ownership can add atomic reference-count operations and contention that become expensive in hot paths.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: Node-based vs. contiguous containers
description: Pointer-heavy containers can have poor cache locality and allocation overhead despite attractive asymptotic complexity.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: `std::unordered_map` performance assumptions
description: Average constant-time complexity hides hashing costs, pointer chasing, rehashing, allocator effects, and pathological collision behavior.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: Custom allocator and `std::pmr` lifetime errors
description: Allocator resources must outlive their dependent allocations, and allocator propagation rules can create unexpected ownership or performance behavior.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: `memcpy` vs. element-wise copying
description: For suitable types, copying raw bytes can be a powerful optimization, but it depends on valid object lifetime, representation, and aliasing assumptions.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: Hidden copies in range-based loops
description: A loop that looks reference-like can accidentally copy expensive objects or proxy values due to type deduction.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: Clock semantics in latency measurement
description: `system_clock`, `steady_clock`, and `high_resolution_clock` have different guarantees; the highest-resolution clock is not necessarily steady.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: I/O buffering and unexpected flushing
description: Standard stream operations can impose synchronization, locale-processing, or flushing costs at surprising points.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: Compile-time vs. runtime computation
description: `constexpr` does not guarantee that every call is evaluated at compile time, while `consteval` imposes stronger constraints.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: Floating-point prices and exact comparisons
description: Binary floating-point cannot represent every decimal financial quantity exactly, creating potentially unacceptable precision and ordering behavior.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: Compiler optimization exploiting undefined behavior
description: Optimizing compilers may eliminate, reorder, or transform operations based on the assumption that undefined behavior never occurs.

category: Low-latency and HFT-specific C++ footguns
title: Microbenchmark distortions
description: Compiler elimination of unused work, inlining differences, optimization barriers, and caching can make C++ microbenchmarks measure something other than the intended operation.
